name: Malawi
summary: Formerly Nyasaland, independent from Britain in 1964; ruled by Hastings Banda until 1994; known as “the warm heart of Africa”.

knownFor.label: Lake Malawi
knownFor.note: Home to hundreds of fish species.

terrain.value: The Great Rift Valley runs through it, holding Lake Malawi; around it are highlands such as the Shire Highlands, Zomba Plateau and Nyika Plateau.

climate.value: Subtropical, with a hot rainy season from November to April and a cooler dry season; cooler in the highlands.

resources.value: Fertile soils for tobacco, tea, sugar and maize, fish from Lake Malawi, and uranium (mined at Kayelekera in 2009–14).

disasters.value: Droughts and floods; Cyclone Freddy (2023) killed more than 1,000 people in the south.

population.value: 21,240,689 in a 2024 estimate (infobox) but 22,224,282 as of July 2025 in the text; 17,563,749 at the 2018 census.

urbanisation.value: Mostly rural, with fewer than a fifth in towns; the main cities are Lilongwe (capital since 1975), Blantyre, Mzuzu and Zomba.

disease.value: HIV/AIDS hit hard from the 1990s; malaria, tuberculosis and cholera outbreaks are also major problems.

migration.value: Many men worked in South African and Zimbabwean mines; in the 1980s–90s Malawi hosted about a million refugees from Mozambique.

economicBase.value: Heavily agricultural: agriculture is 35% of GDP (industry 19%, services 46%) and provides 90% of export revenues; tobacco is the first-listed product.

tradeRoutes.value: As a landlocked country, it sends goods by rail and road to the ports of Beira and Nacala in Mozambique and Dar es Salaam in Tanzania.

wealth.value: HDI 0.517, low (172nd, 2023); about 40% lived below the poverty line in 2006.

moneyAndTax.value: The Malawian kwacha, introduced in 1971 to replace the Malawian pound.

inequality.value: Large gaps between the capital and rural areas.

governmentType.value: A unitary presidential republic; Nyasaland became independent as Malawi on 6 July 1964.

keyRulers.value: Hastings Banda was prime minister in 1963 and president for life from 1971; Bakili Muluzi beat him in 1994 and served to 2004; Bingu wa Mutharika (elected 2004) died in April 2012 and Joyce Banda succeeded him; Lazarus Chakwera won in 2020 and Peter Mutharika returned to power in 2025.

stability.value: No civil war; Banda’s rule (1964–94) was repressive, but the change to multiparty democracy in 1993–94 was peaceful.

eliteConflict.value: Competition between political parties and leaders.

armyAndTech.value: The Malawi Defence Force, a small army that in 1993 disarmed the ruling party’s Young Pioneers and serves in UN peacekeeping.

majorWars.value: No wars of its own; Mozambique’s civil war (1977–92) spilled across its borders and sent refugees into Malawi.

territoryChange.value: No change since 1964; it disputes with Tanzania the border on Lake Malawi (Lake Nyasa).

alliancesRivals.value: A member of SADC, the African Union and the Commonwealth; under Banda it unusually kept diplomatic ties with apartheid South Africa.

inventions.value: No major inventions are associated with the modern state.

scienceEducation.value: Literacy is still limited; the University of Malawi was founded in 1964, and free primary schooling began in 1994.

openness.value: Open to trade and foreign investment, with periods of restriction.

communicationTransport.value: Roads such as the M1 north–south highway, a railway to Mozambique’s ports, and lake ships such as the Ilala on Lake Malawi.

religion.value: The infobox gives 82.3% Christian and 13.8% Muslim (2018 census); the text gives Christianity at 77.3% and government surveys 87%, so the figures conflict.

languageWriting.value: English is official; Chichewa is the national language, with Chitumbuka, Chiyao and others widely spoken.

artsArchitecture.value: Gule Wamkulu masked dances of the Chewa (recognised by UNESCO), wood carving, and music and dance at village ceremonies.

socialStructure.value: Many ethnic groups: Chewa (the largest), Lomwe, Yao, Ngoni, Tumbuka and others; most are smallholder farmers.

sharedIdentity.value: A shared national identity as “the warm heart of Africa”, alongside regional loyalties between north, centre and south.

dailyLife.value: Most live in villages of brick houses; nsima (stiff maize porridge) is eaten with vegetables, beans or chambo fish.

neighbours.value: Tanzania to the north, Zambia to the west, and Mozambique to the south and east.

ideasReligions.value: Christianity, spread by Scottish missions such as Livingstonia and Blantyre from the 1870s, Islam, and Chewa traditions.

colonisation.value: The British Central African Protectorate from 1891, renamed Nyasaland in 1907; independent on 6 July 1964.

riseSignals.value: Independence from Britain on 6 July 1964; a republic from 1966 under Hastings Banda.

peakPeriod.value: Too recent to judge; growth was strong in the late 1960s–70s and again in the mid-2000s with farm subsidies.

declineSignals.value: None that define the country as a whole.

outcome.value: Still in existence as an independent republic.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
